correctness.computation_scope: Exact exhaustive finite theorem for one labeled 14-vertex complex; no sampling or timeout inference.
correctness.rationale: The published 41-facet simplicial complex has face vector (14,66,94,41). Exact finite recursion evaluates non-evasiveness for every deletion and link, giving all 14 admissible first vertices and second-step counts (11 repeated 6 times, 9 repeated 4 times, 5 repeated 4 times), total 122. A separate bitmask maximal-face enumeration reproduces all numerical claims and 28,708 memoized recursion states.

evidence: Theorem 6.2 in Benedetti--Lutz proves vertex-decomposable balls are non-evasive; Rudin ball is specifically not vertex-decomposable.
Related exact first-root classifications in other triangulations concern different complexes.

originality.rationale: Benedetti--Lutz Theorem 6.3 proves the same Rudin ball non-evasive using a single first vertex (3) and a specified sequence. It does not assert all 14 admissible roots or count admissible second roots. Exact-object public catalogs provide facets and global topological properties, not the two-query census. No stronger covering statement was found; indexed-search limitations remain.
residual_risks: Older non-indexed computation might already give the root profile.
No guarantee of exhaustive bibliographic priority is claimed.

scope: The finding is confined to the canonical published triangulation; no claim about arbitrary non-evasive balls or complete witness trees.

value.rationale: The famous Rudin ball is a standard finite test object distinguishing non-evasiveness, shellability and vertex-decomposability. Every initial vertex being allowable strengthens the established existence claim in a structural way; the 11/9/5 second-choice stratification quantifies the earliest nonuniform decision-tree behavior. It is a natural exact invariant of a benchmark triangulation rather than an arbitrary numerical slice.
